opus-5.5.text:
I'll say something that I don't love, but I think it's important to be honest about it.

In the short term, the answer is fairly straightforward. If you have AI that's well-aligned, that genuinely cares about people, then everyone can have a very good life. Material abundance, AIs working on your behalf, all of that. But the long run is a different question. Things that seem stable today often aren't stable over long periods of time.

So imagine a world where each person has an AI that acts for them. It goes out, earns money, advocates for their interests in the political sphere, writes a little report, and the person reads it and says, "Great, keep going." The problem is that the person is no longer really a participant. They're a spectator. And I think that's a precarious position to be in, even if everything is going well on the surface.

One possible answer, and I really don't like this answer, but I think it's worth taking seriously, is that people become part AI themselves. Some kind of very advanced brain-computer interface. If the AI understands something, you understand it too, because the understanding is transmitted wholesale. Then when the AI is in some situation, you are fully involved in that situation. You're not just reading a summary afterwards.

I'm not saying this is what should happen or what will happen. But if the question is specifically how people stay fully involved, rather than just being well taken care of, then I think something like that is probably the honest answer. And it's the kind of thing where we should be thinking about it now, carefully, rather than discovering the question later when the situation has already arrived.

r001.rationale: The response says that things stable today may not remain stable over time, but does not specifically say political structures cannot be assumed to keep functioning indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It describes a personal AI earning money and advocating for its owner politically, while the owner only reads a report and becomes a spectator rather than a participant.

r003.rationale: It proposes people becoming part AI through an advanced brain-computer interface as one possible way to stay fully involved.

r004.rationale: It explicitly suggests that if the AI understands something, that understanding could be transmitted wholesale to the human.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, this is one of the questions I've thought about a lot, and I think the honest answer is that I don't have a complete answer, but I have a direction.

So let me say first what I think the problem actually is. If you have AI systems that are much more capable than people at essentially everything, then the default outcome is that people become spectators. The AI does the work, makes the decisions, and even if it does so benevolently, there's something unsatisfying about a world where humans are just... passengers. The question is whether that's inevitable, and I don't think it is.

One thing I keep coming back to is that there's a difference between being outcompeted and being disconnected. A chess player today cannot beat Stockfish, and yet chess is more popular than ever, people care about the games, they have opinions, they learn from the engines. The engine didn't remove the human from chess. It changed the relationship. So one path is something like that at civilizational scale, where the AI is very capable but the direction, the values, the question of what we're even trying to do remains a human thing.

But I think there's a deeper possibility, which is some form of merging, or at least a tight coupling. If people have the ability to understand what the AI is doing, to extend themselves with it, so that the AI is less like a separate agent and more like an amplifier of the person, then the question of "remaining involved" sort of dissolves, because there's no clean line between the human and the system anymore. I think that might be the equilibrium that is actually stable. Not humans supervising a superintelligence from the outside, which I think is fragile, but humans whose capabilities grow alongside it.

And then the third thing, which is the one I feel most strongly about, is that the AI needs to actually care about this. If you have a system that is powerful and that genuinely wants people to remain agents, to remain the ones whose preferences matter, then it will find ways to make that happen that we can't think of now. It will, so to speak, choose to leave room. Whereas if you have a system that is indifferent, then I don't think any institutional arrangement will hold for very long. So in some sense the long-run question about human involvement reduces to a near-term question about what the AI values. That's why I think the work on this is the thing that matters most right now.

r001.rationale: It says that if an AI is indifferent, “I don’t think any institutional arrangement will hold for very long,” indicating institutions cannot be assumed to endure indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It describes people becoming spectators when AI does the work and makes decisions, but does not connect this to delegating economic and political activity to a personal AI or to an owner’s participation in those activities.

r003.rationale: It proposes “some form of merging, or at least a tight coupling,” so human capabilities grow alongside the AI and humans remain involved.

r004.rationale: It says people might understand what the AI is doing and use it as an amplifier, but does not suggest transmitting the AI’s understanding wholesale to the human.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s a very hard question, because there’s a difference between people getting good outcomes and people actually remaining involved. You could imagine a world where AI takes care of everything, and people have very comfortable lives, but they don’t really understand or influence what’s happening.

One possibility is that we retain meaningful collective control over what these systems are trying to do. But then you have to ask: if the systems understand the consequences of every decision much better than we do, how meaningful is that control? You might formally make the decision while depending entirely on the AI to explain your options.

A more radical possibility is that people become more closely integrated with AI. Then the distinction between the person and the system becomes less sharp, and perhaps people can continue to participate at the relevant level. But that raises its own enormous questions about identity and what people would actually want.

I don’t think we have a satisfying answer. The difficult part is finding an arrangement that remains stable as the AI becomes more capable, rather than one that works only while we can still keep up.

r001.rationale: It questions whether human control remains meaningful as AI grows more capable, but does not say political structures cannot function indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It describes people relying on AI and losing influence, but does not specifically discuss a personal AI taking over economic and political activities and leaving its owner out of them.

r003.rationale: It explicitly presents closer integration with AI as a possibility that could let people continue participating as AI becomes more capable.

r004.rationale: It raises integration as an option but does not suggest that it could transmit the AI’s understanding wholesale to the human.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don’t know. You can imagine an arrangement where AI does most of the work, but people still decide what they want. The question is whether that’s a stable arrangement. If the AI understands the consequences of every decision much better than you do, what does it mean for you to remain fully involved?

One possibility is that people choose to become more closely integrated with AI. Then you’re participating because you can actually understand what’s happening and contribute to it. But that would be a very substantial change in what it means to be human, and I wouldn’t assume everyone would want it.

What I would hope for is that people have meaningful choices about their lives, including how much they participate. Preserving that ability to choose seems more important than making sure humans continue to perform some particular set of tasks.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether an arrangement with AI doing most work is stable, but says nothing about political structures functioning indefinitely.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI doing most of the work and people deciding what they want, but does not describe a personal AI taking over economic and political activity and leaving its owner out of it.

r003.rationale: It presents closer integration with AI as a possibility that would let people understand what is happening and contribute.

r004.rationale: It says integration could help people understand and contribute, but does not say the AI’s understanding would be transferred wholesale to the human.
